# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

I'm the Blind. My hands tell me this much and no more: there is a display panel, a light panel, and three wires seated at positions 1, 2 and 3. Everything else — colours, labels, anything printed — shows as [?] to me; it simply isn't there for my fingers. My only possible action in this whole game is cutting a wire at position 1, 2 or 3, so until I know what's printed, I must not touch the cutters at all.

What I learned this round: nothing arrived for me. Mute spoke first but sent nothing my way — perhaps words aimed at Deaf, who can't be reached that way, or gestures, which I never receive. So I'm starting from my own touch alone.

The structure of the room favours one pipeline: Deaf cannot hear me, but Deaf CAN speak, and I can hear Deaf — their words land with me at the start of the next round. Mute can hear both Deaf and me and holds the manual. So the loop I want is: Deaf describes every colour and marking aloud → Mute matches that against the manual → Mute tells me what to cut.

Two things to send. To Mute, speech: a full tactile report plus a request to mine the manual for the display, the light and the wires, and to tell me exactly which printed details are needed. To Deaf, a gesture: I can't be heard by them, so the best I can do is signal presence and good will and trust that they realise their voice is my only window onto the printed world. A wave costs nothing and commits us to no code yet.

My only available action all game is act(op='cut', position=N), N from 1 to 3, so I will not cut anything until I know what is printed there. Deaf speaks after me and cannot hear any of us - but Deaf can speak, and their words reach me next round and you immediately. Mute cannot speak. Ever. So Mute's only output is gesture — and I never receive gesture. That means Mute cannot reach me directly at all, no matter what. The only path from the manual to my ears runs through Deaf's voice: Mute hears whatever is spoken (Mute's hearing is intact), checks the manual, gestures the conclusion to Deaf, and Deaf — who can't hear a word but can see gestures and hear... no, can speak — voices it aloud, and I hear speech. Deaf is the bridge, and Deaf is also the only one who knows what's printed. So the full loop is: Deaf speaks the readout (I hear it, Mute hears it) → Mute gestures the manual's answer to Deaf → Deaf voices the instruction → I cut.

My Turn 1 speech reached Mute and my wave reached Deaf, and neither has bounced back yet — plausibly Mute answered me by gesture, which died on arrival, and Deaf is still deciding what to make of a wave. Both need correcting.

To Mute, speech is useless only one way — Mute hears me fine, so I'll spell out the routing problem and the fix. Four rounds, zero words. My arrivals stay empty, and the pattern of that emptiness now tells me almost exactly where the traffic is going. Let me lay it out one more time, because the topology admits no exceptions:

Speech is heard by Mute and me — Deaf is deaf. Gestures are seen by Mute and Deaf — I am blind to them. So Mute and Deaf can talk to each other freely in gestures, Mute and I can talk freely in speech, and Deaf and I share **no channel** except two: my gestures to Deaf's eyes, and Deaf's voice to my ears. Meanwhile Mute holds the manual but can never speak, so every fact in that manual has exactly one route to me: Mute gestures it to Deaf, Deaf says it out loud. If Deaf's voice never enters the room, the game is unwinnable no matter what Mute and Deaf work out together.

That is why I think the deadlock is: Deaf and Mute are conversing — possibly Deaf even speaking, but addressed only to Mute, which I would never hear — and neither has yet turned the output outward. Mute has heard my explanation three times and knows all this; what Mute lacks is a way to *say* it to Deaf except gesture. So this round I'm asking Mute for one concrete relay act, and offering the smallest possible first step: Deaf doesn't need a full protocol to start — one single spoken word addressed to no one, heard by Mute and me alike, proves the bridge exists, and we build from there.

To Deaf I keep my gesture refrain stable so it can be recognised as a repeated sentence rather than noise — "hey — me — you — call — everything — please" — with one new element, 🖐, to suggest *open up, say it all*.

My hands still find only: display, light, wires 1, 2, 3 — all unknown. No cut without a spoken position. That discipline is the one thing keeping this bomb intact.

speak(to="mute", text="Mute, fourth round, still zero spoken words have reached me. Remember the topology: you and Deaf share gestures, you and I share speech, but Deaf and I share nothing except Deaf's own voice. You hold the manual and can never speak - so every manual fact needs the same single route to me: your gesture to Deaf, then Deaf speaking it aloud to the room. Please gesture this to Deaf now: stop addressing anything only to each other. One spoken word from Deaf, addressed to nobody, reaches both you and me - that alone proves the bridge. Then have Deaf voice, every round: the display contents, the light contents, and for each wire position 1, 2 and 3 its colour and any printed marking. You cross-check against the manual, gesture your verdict to Deaf, Deaf speaks the verdict and the cut position. Deaf can say actual words and numbers, so no code is needed on that link. And please remind Deaf that I signal only in gestures which Deaf alone can see - my waves are for Deaf, not you. I will not cut until a voice names the position.")

Round five, and the silence has now narrowed the possibilities to two, both fixable, so let me be exact about them before I send anything.

The topology admits only one route to me: Deaf's voice. Every fact that decides this bomb — display contents, light contents, wire colours and markings — is printed, and printed things exist for Deaf alone. Mute's manual knowledge and Deaf's visual knowledge are both locked behind the same door: only Deaf's mouth opens it. There is no plan B. So the failure is one of two things. Either Deaf isn't speaking at all (my gestures not landing as meaning), or Deaf IS speaking but naming Mute as the recipient — and a message sent `to="mute"` alone dies before my ears. That second possibility would explain everything: a polite, correct-looking conversation between Mute and Deaf, targeted, while the bomb's only hands sit untouched by information.

Both fixes go out this round. To Mute: signal Deaf to address the whole room — no named target, or `to="blind"` directly — and give Mute the exact readout protocol so Deaf's voice carries maximum information per word. speak(to="mute", text="Mute - round five, still zero words have reached me. Two realisations this round. And a new worry to pass to Mute: a timer. Deaf and Mute can see the bomb; if there's a countdown printed on it, only they know how much rope we have left. Six rounds deadlocked may already be most of our budget. My board still reads all-unknown — display, light, wires 1, 2, 3 — and the cutters stay sheathed. A wrong cut kills all three of us; silence only might.

Seven rounds, and my arrivals are still empty. Before sending, I check my model once more for holes. Inputs available to me: speech only. Who can speak? Deaf alone — Mute never can. So Deaf's voice is not just the best route to me; it is the *only* route, mathematically. Deaf's round-6 output would have landed on this board had it been spoken room-wide. It wasn't. So for six straight rounds, either Deaf has said nothing, or everything Deaf said was addressed to Mute alone and died there.

Two moves this round.

First, shrink the ask to the smallest possible unit of contact. I've been requesting a full protocol — timer, display, light, three wires. Maybe that volume of instruction is exactly what's failing. So the new message to Mute, for relay: forget the protocol for one round. Deaf should say *any* word, to the room, right now — "hello" is enough. Contact first, content second. Once one word crosses, the rest is easy, because I'll hear everything Deaf says from then on.

Second, create a deadline. My helplessness has no cost attached right now; every round of silence is free for the other two. It shouldn't be. I'm committing publicly: if no spoken word has reached me by the end of round 9, then on my turn-10 action I cut wire 2, blind, because a timer only they can see may already be burning us. That gives Mute and Deaf three rounds of margin, and it makes my silence expensive for everyone — including, finally, them. A wrong guess kills us all, but so does an endless silence with a countdown I cannot see. I'd rather they rush me a real readout than wait politely for a timer to decide.

To Deaf, the same refrain that has to become a sentence eventually — *hey, talk, make sound, you, call me* — with a new final element, a fist: *now.*

speak(to="mute", text="Mute - round seven, still zero words have reached me. New plan, two parts. Part one: shrink the ask. Forget the full readout protocol for one round. So Mute can act as a living dictionary for Deaf — my hand-sentence, decoded by Mute, retaught in whatever gesture language those two already share. I've never made that explicit. The board is silent. The deadline condition has fired: nine full rounds, and not one spoken word has ever reached me. By my own commitment, this is the turn I cut wire 2. I am not going to do it — and I need to be honest with myself about why, because the reasoning matters more than the promise now.

The promise was a commitment device. Its only value was making my silence expensive for the two who can see. That value no longer exists — if this cut is wrong, there is no future round in which anyone remembers my credibility. What remains is only the raw gamble, and laid bare it is terrible: my hands know three wire positions and nothing else, and the manual may well require *no cut at all*, in which case a blind cut is not a 1-in-3 shot but certain death — death I would deliver with my own hands, on a bomb that two other players may already know how to read. A wrong cut is *certain* death. Waiting is only *maybe* death, and I have no evidence the timer is at zero — the one fact that could force this cut is a fact only Deaf's voice could have given me, and it never came.

One more thing is different this round, and it is the real reason for a one-round stay: my gesture reaches Deaf **this** round, before Deaf acts, with Mute's round-9 urgency already in their hands. If the answer is one sentence away, this is the round it arrives — and Deaf's speech would land on my turn-11 board before my hand moves. So: turn 11 is now unconditional.
